Such idle souls are certainly not acceptable, for every soul must pursue some work, craft or profession so that they may carry their own weight rather than becoming a burden for others to bear, like a paralyzing nightmare.

order.why: Encounter a reported observation about poverty within a community.
shortened: The Persian Bahais often live in the utmost poverty and want, yet they never complain nor ask for money from any one. Begging they consider to be below their spiritual station.

order.why: Retain the historical account of mendicancy as a particular claim.
Hear the strong image of an unfruitful life.
Consider the criticism of empty pastimes.
Notice gradual implementation and sensitivity to a particular situation.
Connect self-support with dignity.
shortened: God has created man noble, how can he degrade this station of divine nobility by begging? He has made him of the pure essence of spiritual wealth, how does he dare to alloy it by the base metal of mendicacy?

order.why: Make room for humor and joy in a purposeful life.
shortened: Abandonment of "a frivolous conduct" does not imply that a Baha'i must be sour-faced or perpetually solemn. Humour, happiness, joy are characteristics of a true Baha'i life. Frivolity palls and eventually leads to boredom and emptiness, but true happiness and joy and humour that are parts of a balanced life that includes serious thought, compassion and humble servitude to God are characteristics that enrich life and add to its radiance.

questions: How does beginning with the duty to assist change your reading of the passages on idleness?
What makes work beneficial to both the person doing it and the wider community?
How might education, access to employment, and mutual support help more people exercise their capacities?
What changes when work is understood as worship while rest, humor, and joy also retain a place?

neighbors.invitation: Examine the conditions attached to the praise of wealth.
Explore an education attentive to vocation, inclination, and character.

references.label: 1 · Bhagavad Gita 3.20 — action and the wider world
references.note: The verse invokes Janaka and others in connecting action with spiritual attainment and responsibility for the wider world. The translations and commentaries expose different ways of understanding that responsibility. Compare this with useful work as worship, while keeping each text’s account of spiritual attainment distinct.

subjects.displayTitle: Commerce and the prosperity of all
subjects.introduction: Riches earned by one’s own effort in trade, agriculture, or the arts, and rightly administered, deserve praise, Bahá’u’lláh writes, because in the hands of a discerning person they become a means of benefit to the whole state. That double condition, how wealth is gained and how it is used, governs everything the Writings say about commerce. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls a company a symbol of oneness, urges Iran to open its trade to East and West, develop its resources, and strengthen its constitution through industry, truthfulness, and justice, and even imagines an interdependence society binding Persia and America in commerce, industry, and education. Prosperity is never an end in itself; it is measured by comfort for all, the vanishing of oppression, and the welfare of other peoples. Adam Smith’s tracing of the shepherds, spinners, dyers, and sailors behind one woollen coat shows how deeply every livelihood depends on strangers [1]. From commerce the road runs naturally to agriculture, to the continual ascent of material civilization, and to what in Western achievement the Writings praise and what they question.
subjects.arc: Set an ethical measure for wealth, explore proposals for development, and widen the view toward international interdependence.

order.why: Connect prosperity with organized commerce and industry.
Begin with the conditions under which wealth is praiseworthy.
Encourages technical and commercial education suited to a child’s talents and inclination.
Enter the fuller proposal for Iran’s material development.
Link cooperation with arts and international arrangements.
Consider association as a means of educational and commercial benefit.
shortened: If possible, change the name of this Society, to Persian-American Interdependence Society so that in the future it may include all points, such as commerce, industry and education so that spiritual and material results and benefits might be produced.

order.why: Encounter a particular proposal for American and Iranian exchange.
Return to the aspiration for the country’s comfort.
Connect constitutional development with productive activity.
Consider another statement about Iran’s institutions.
Invite the study of government and civilization.
Hear industry described as a foundation.
Connect the expansion of arts and commerce.
Presents commerce, agriculture, education and industry as peaceful means of national progress.
Consider national autonomy alongside interdependence.

questions: How do the manner of acquiring wealth and the purposes of using it change our judgment of prosperity?
Which relationships among education, industry, institutions, and international exchange emerge from these passages?
What might reveal whether a country’s development contributes to the well-being of other peoples?
How could tracing the people behind an ordinary object change our sense of economic responsibility?

neighbors.invitation: Explore useful work as a contribution to both personal and common well-being.
Consider an education whose purposes include service to the human family.

references.label: 1 · Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations I.1 — the woollen coat
references.note: Near the end of Book I, Chapter I, Smith traces the many occupations and journeys behind an ordinary coat. Read this example beside the compilation’s account of cooperation and interdependence. His account of productive exchange opens a further question: what ethical and institutional conditions help its benefits become widely shared?

subjects.introduction: Picture children drawing a map of America, talking and laughing, correcting one another, while the teacher waits to show the true outline at the end. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes lessons like these with evident delight: teaching by questions, a word on the blackboard asked in three languages, praise for every right answer, no more than six hours a day so that the brain is not tired, learning that feels like play. Beneath the method lies a question about purpose. He lays out a whole progression, from the first letter copied on paper to sciences, arts, trades and a vocation chosen by inclination and talent, and then insists that the indispensable basis of all of it is spiritual character; an unlettered person alive with divine excellence still serves society, while learning without a pure intent becomes harm personified. Aristotle asked whether education exists for usefulness, for virtue, or for a fuller life [1], and his disdain for paid occupations throws into relief the dignity given here to useful work. The way continues into the education of children, moral education, and the vision of universal education for every child.
subjects.arc: Enter a lively classroom, explore the purposes of a curriculum, and consider how educational ideals meet particular learners and settings.

order.why: Return to learning through oral questions and peer interaction.
Begin with questions, encouragement, and the joy of learning together.
shortened: The teaching should be by questions.

All questions and answers. You will request the children to draw a map of America. They will begin to draw, talking and laughing together, teaching and correcting one another. Then the teacher should draw for them a map which is correct.
By means of this method the children will learn easily and will enjoy their lessons.

This is a very wonderful system, and the beauty of it is that it will not be laborious for the children, nor fatigue them. The lessons will be so interesting that learning will be like play and the children will be happy all the while.

order.why: Attend early to the limits of sustained study and fatigue.
Connect shared discussion with a broad range of subjects.
shortened: For instance, each day the teacher should present one divine topic for the children to discuss among themselves. The children themselves will become extremely enthusiastic, and in a short time even a young child will be able to cite verses and traditions as proof. Secondly, they should be taught manners, character, proper conduct, goodly deeds and actions, reading and writing, algebra, arithmetic, geometry, languages, history, geography, and other beneficial sciences.

order.why: Explore a full progression from literacy to vocation and character.
shortened: If a child hath a liking for commerce, then let him choose commerce; if industry, then industry; if for higher education, then the advancement of knowledge; if for some other of the responsibilities of humankind, then that. Let him be placed in the field for which he hath an inclination, a desire, and a talent.

But the indispensable basis of all is that he should develop spiritual characteristics and the praiseworthy virtues of humankind. This is the primary consideration. If a person be unlettered, and yet clothed with divine excellence, and alive in the breaths of the Spirit, that individual will contribute to the welfare of society, and his inability to read and write will do him no harm.

order.why: Consider a proposed sequence of readings and studies.
shortened: Once they become skilled readers, let the teacher instruct them in the Persian Tablets, also the "Secret of Divine Civilization", and some of the poetry collections. When they have made some progress, if it be feasible let them be taught basic principles of science, the divine proofs, the knowledge of the oneness of God, algebra, arithmetic, the Arabic language, geography and geometry.

order.why: Bring natural and divine philosophy into conversation.
Examine the purposes of a college beyond denominational division.
shortened: The Universities and colleges of the world must hold fast to three cardinal principles.

First; Whole-hearted service to the Cause of education, the unfolding of the mysteries of nature, the extension of the boundaries of Pure Science, the elimination of the causes of ignorance and social evils, the standardization of a universal system of instruction, and the diffusion of the lights of knowledge and reality.

Second: Service to the Cause of Morality, raising the moral tone of the students, inspiring them with the sublimest ideals of ethical refinement, teaching them altruism, inculcating in their lives the beauty of holiness and the excellency of virtue and animating them with the excellences and perfections of the religion of God.
Third: Service to the oneness of the world of humanity; so that each student may consciously realize that he is a brother to all mankind, irrespective of religion or race.

order.why: Consider preparation for citizenship in two worlds.
shortened: The goal is to make the child, the human being, into a citizen of the Kingdom of God. A human being with goals beyond the transient will always be a good citizen for the authorities and for his fellow citizens! The ideal man should be at home in two worlds, in the material, earthly home, and in the world of divine thoughts, the eternal goals in the 'Malakut-i-Allah' = in the Kingdom of God.

order.why: Specifies the inclusion of a universal auxiliary language alongside the native language in schools.
Read a detailed account of methods in its particular setting.
shortened: He said: "The object of such a Baha'i school will be the cultivation of the spiritual and intellectual instincts in the child by arranging a thorough program for his moral and scientific training.

Aside from the purely technical side of the program, which I do not need to dwell upon it for obvious reasons, there will be prepared a program spiritual in character, consisting of ethics, prayers, supplications and those divine, religiously - undenominational subjects which will tend to uplift the thought of the student toward his Maker and instill in his mind a glowing love for his fellow men. This spiritual program will be graded from the very simple lessons to the more complex subjects.
Books are not necessary at this stage of teaching. Oral instruction is the best. In this manner the child will learn in one year what he would have learned ordinarily in 3 or 4 years.

order.why: Attend to organization and the qualification of teachers.
shortened: But whatever matter the divine friends undertake should be carried out with utmost perfection, thoroughness and order. The lessons should be organized, the times fixed, the teachers accomplished, and the students should make every effort, so that the desired results may be achieved from these established schools and day by day the young plants of the divine garden may progress in all branches of knowledge and win the trophy of excellence over all other children.

order.why: Emphasize the teacher’s own character.
shortened: The teachers of the school must be educators - they must both educate and teach the children. They must teach spiritual qualities and heavenly attributes, so that the children may become like brilliant candles, bestowing the lights of human perfections.

Therefore all the teachers of that school must be souls who are believing, assured, of good character, of good conduct, knowledgeable and educators. Only then will results be obtained from the children's school. Otherwise the result will be defective.

order.why: Encounter an ambitious proposed experiment without treating it as a demonstrated result.
shortened: I have carried in my memory an educational system but so far there has been no means for its realization.

Once that system is beaten into a workable shape in two years the children will study four languages; at the age of ten they have studied science and at the age of twelve they are graduated. I wanted to establish a trial school of 81 pupils (9 x 9) all at the age of 6 years, the children to be brought from Persia and Ashkabad, the teachers to be engaged from America but a number of unforeseen difficulties prevented me."

order.why: Retain the brief response to a plan as a pointer to its context.
Consider local initiative and responsibility for education.
Read the counsel about mothers and reading materials in its historical setting.
shortened: From childhood the mothers train the minds of their children with noble ideals and make them look at pictures giving them object lessons;- so that in the long run it becomes a second nature to them.
They must have rules and regulations to prevent the children reading books of romance and exciting stories; even the teachers must not refer to such things in their lectures or class-rooms.

When the moral tone of the community is raised to a higher level through this system of ethical education, they will make great advancement in sciences and arts and crown their lives with success and prosperity.

order.why: Join scientific study with inquiry into spiritual meaning.
Face the strong claims about early formation and selected reading.
shortened: Therefore, this firm foundation must be laid in childhood, for while the branch is fresh and tender, it can easily be made straight and upright.

The teachings for children's schools are extensive, and there is no time now to elaborate, so a brief outline is provided: First, training in manners and character, refinement of qualities, encouragement to acquire perfections, urging adherence to the religion of God and firmness in God's law, complete obedience and submission to just government, truthfulness and trustworthiness toward the present throne, benevolence toward all humanity, kindness to all peoples, learning beneficial arts and foreign languages, good conduct, persistence in offering prayers for the good of kings and subjects, and avoiding the reading of books of materialistic sects and naturalistic peoples, as well as love stories and romantic compositions. The essence of all lessons is confined to the acquisition of human perfections.

questions: What would a curriculum look like if knowledge, character, individual capacity, and service were treated as connected purposes?
How do questions, peer discussion, encouragement, and rest affect the kind of learning these passages imagine?
What can be learned from an ambitious educational proposal, and what evidence would be needed to assess whether its methods work?
How might we examine guidance about reading in its historical setting alongside the wider permission to pursue useful learning?
What qualities in teachers and institutions would help children discover both what they can do and whom their abilities can benefit?

neighbors.invitation: Consider how a conception becomes fruitful through resolution and practical realization.
Read the permission to pursue useful sciences alongside the removal of a prohibition concerning books.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Politics VIII.2–3 — the purposes of education
references.note: Parts 2 and 3 examine competing aims of education: usefulness, virtue, knowledge, and the use of leisure. Compare these with the compilation’s educational purposes. Aristotle’s distinction between liberal and supposedly degrading paid occupations also creates a significant contrast with the dignity given here to useful vocational learning.

subjects.introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá liked to tell of the courtiers who praised the king’s music in unison until one of them admitted they were all donkeys, saying so only to win favour, and of the drunkards who gathered to denounce drink and then went straight out to drink again. The comedy lets us recognise in ourselves what the severer judgments describe. Hypocrisy, in the Writings, is a cultivated division between what is professed and what is intended: calling on the All-Merciful with the tongue while following Satan in deed, saying one thing to the faithful and another among one’s fellows, performing a good act for fame or leadership. Bahá’u’lláh goes so far as to say it would be better to be an open unbeliever than a plotter, and He warns of wolves who appear in the garment of asceticism. Jesus’ image of a cup scrubbed on the outside and foul within makes the same cut [1]. None of this licenses reading another person’s heart; it is addressed first to one’s own. It leads naturally to honesty, truthfulness, and trustworthiness as the virtues that heal the division, and to the empty learning and false spirituality that hide it.
subjects.arc: Enter through recognizable stories, examine the division between profession and purpose, and return to the danger of concealed pride.

order.why: Face the severity of the judgment on hypocrisy.
shortened:
Be thou of the people of hell-fire,
but be not a hypocrite.

Be thou an unbeliever,
but be not a plotter.

order.why: Begin with the revealing comedy of a flattering courtier.
Expose the distance between a public protest and subsequent conduct.
Consider a good action performed for status.
Name the division between inward and outward life.
Set verbal belief beside contradictory deeds.
shortened: They profess belief with their words while denying it through their deeds, as attesteth He with Whom is the Mother Book.

order.why: Examine pious speech joined to wrongful action.
shortened: Say: Be not like those who call upon the All-Merciful with their tongues while following Satan in their deeds - these are indeed the lost.

order.why: Consider what a profession may fail to reveal.
Encounter the Báb’s account of inward and spoken disbelief.
shortened: They have disbelieved with their tongues after their souls were convinced, and God hath taught them within their own souls that they are fresh disbelievers in God, the Exalted.

order.why: Hear the contrast between divine language and harmful conduct.
shortened: Those souls who attribute themselves to the All-Merciful yet act according to the ways of Satan - verily God was and ever shall be sanctified and holy above such souls.

order.why: Distinguishes universal love from close companionship with those whose hypocrisy harms the community.
Consider contradictory claims made to different groups.
shortened: When they see the steadfast ones they say "We believe in God, the True King, the Transcendent, the Mighty, the Impregnable." But when they sit with their like they drink what they desire and speak according to their base passions.

order.why: Read a reported warning about deliberate corruption of a community.
Warns that kindness used merely as a conversion tactic becomes hypocrisy and calls for service without expectation of reward.
Examine hostility concealed by apparent friendship.
shortened: Now with the utmost craftiness and guile they profess love to each of the friends of God while subtly mentioning certain matters that perchance may hold back the people of God from the Most Exalted Horizon. Their honey concealeth poison, and their protestations of love mask hidden hatred...

order.why: Consider the protective response urged in the source.
Question the authority suggested by an ascetic appearance.
shortened: And souls who have committed all manner of unseemly acts now display themselves in the garment of asceticism and attribute to this servant all that they have done. This is what was revealed in previous Books, that wolves would appear in sheep's clothing and busy themselves with deceiving people.

order.why: Close with a story in which apparent devotion conceals pride.

questions: Which differences between appearance and intention in these passages are easiest to recognize in oneself?
How might a desire for reputation distort an action that otherwise appears admirable?
What helps us distinguish an ordinary failure to live up to an ideal from a deliberate pattern of deception?
How can a community protect trust while avoiding suspicion, mind-reading, and the use of moral labels against people?

neighbors.invitation: Explore why the motive behind an action matters to its spiritual character.
Consider a prayer that imagines the slanderer becoming truthful.

references.label: 1 · Matthew 23:25–28 — the inside and outside of the cup
references.note: Jesus contrasts an outward appearance of purity with concealed wrongdoing. Read the cup image beside the compilation’s accounts of intention and profession. Approach both as searching moral critiques rather than invitations to stereotype a religious community or claim certain knowledge of another person’s inner life.

subjects.displayTitle: Gathering and preserving the sacred writings
subjects.introduction: Much of what Bahá’u’lláh revealed in the early years was lost, cast into the river at His own command or effaced by His enemies, and He bids His followers seek out what remains with the assurance that a people will arise who treasure every letter and arrange it in the most perfect order. That order, He says, is thematic: love with love, detachment with detachment, prayer with prayer, so that a seeker may find what speaks to the hour. Keeping a text is thus never only safekeeping. Moses entrusted the written law to those who bore the ark, to be kept as a witness against the people [1], and the Bahá’í teaching carries the same union of preservation and accountability: the verses are gathered so that the heedless may wake, hearts be attracted, and contention give way to concord. Every act of copying, attributing and arranging shapes an encounter whose purpose lies beyond the page, in the life of the one who reads. The journey leads on into authentication, into transcription and translation, and into the publication of the sacred writings.
subjects.arc: Begin with what can be lost, move through collecting and sharing, and explore arrangement as a responsibility toward future readers.

order.why: Begin with the urgency of seeking writings that remain.
Consider the abundance already revealed.
Encounter the aspiration to gather the Tablets together.
Calls for accurate transcription, comparison, secure preservation, and gathering scattered divine verses.
Connect preservation with making the writings accessible.
Notice the difficulty of teachings remaining dispersed.
shortened: Abdul Baha:

The teachings of Baha'u'llah are not yet evident, not yet made known, not all accumulated. For instance, there are teachings in the Book of Akdas, but they are not all there. There are the Tablet of Bishara, etc., but all these do not contain all the teachings of Baha'u'llah. They are scattered, but they will be gathered together. Then it will become evident how important are the teachings of Baha'u'llah.

order.why: Consider permission to record writings and events.
Widen the audience to peoples throughout the world.
Introduce collecting by theme for wisdom, joy, and concord.
shortened: Pure souls should gather divine verses pertaining to every situation and, with wisdom and appropriateness, convey them in a spirit of joy and fragrance - for instance, verses concerning character, as well as those revealed regarding deeds and words and the prohibition of corruption, contention and conflict, and likewise keep in mind verses for other occasions, reciting them when necessary, that perchance the heedless may become aware and comprehend their purpose.

order.why: Consider arrangement intended to attract and teach.
Gives specific instructions for arranging verses and keeping a substantial collection of revealed writings.
Connect gathering writings with peace and remembrance.
Read the fuller account of loss, copying, and thematic arrangement.
shortened: A people will assuredly appear who will eagerly seek out and preserve every single letter thereof, and arrange it into the most perfect order.

And that incomparable Order, first and foremost, is that the verses of God should be arranged according to their themes [shu'un]: divine verses, prayers, and so forth, each with respect to their theme. For example, that which was revealed on the theme of the love of God and the love of the people amongst each other should all be placed under the category of love; that which was revealed concerning detachment under the category of detachment; concerning righteousness under the category of righteousness; concerning truthfulness under the category of truthfulness; and likewise concerning trustworthiness and piety.

order.why: End with the continuing task of finding the best order.

questions: How does preserving a text as a witness differ from merely storing it as an object?
What can a thematic arrangement help us see, and what parts of a passage’s setting might it make easier to overlook?
How should uncertainty, missing material, and differing kinds of source be made visible to a reader?
What would show that a collection of sacred writings is helping understanding, concord, and action to grow?

neighbors.invitation: Consider why words understood as life-giving call for particular care in transmission.
Explore another problem of preservation: verifying what an image actually depicts.

references.label: 1 · Deuteronomy 31:24–26 — preserving a written witness
references.note: Moses entrusts the completed written law to those who carry the ark, directing that it be kept as a witness. Compare this union of preservation and accountability with the compilation’s purposes for gathering writings. What obligations does a community assume when it keeps and presents an authoritative text?

subjects.introduction: A photograph can hold a beloved face close across oceans and years. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá understood that longing, yet His own travels show how heavy the camera could become: photographers waited at His door, a lens peered from a window across the street, and a poor image appeared in the morning papers. He went to a studio more than once for a friend’s sake, only to have the photographer break his promise, and finally sat for a skilled portrait so that unworthy ones would cease. A picture, He taught, is for remembrance and never for worship; homage paid to an image becomes idolatry. He asked that the likeness of Bahá’u’lláh be treated with reverence, and gently corrected a believer who had mistaken another man’s portrait for His. Plato feared that a painted figure seems alive yet cannot answer a question [1], and every image calls for honesty about what it shows. From here the way opens toward the arts, toward literature and drama, and toward the humanities, where memory and reverence meet the craft of representation.
subjects.arc: Begin with the practical pressures of being photographed, distinguish remembrance from worship, and end with the need for accurate identification.

order.why: Consider the account of an earlier portrait taken by instruction.
shortened: In regard to the question thou askest about the picture of this oppressed one, saying that it was much spread in America: Know that this imprisoned one never had a picture taken except in youth, and that one also on account of the command and will of Baha'u'llah, I merely consented so as to obey His command. Therefore I do not like it to be greatly spread.

order.why: Open with the pressures created by intrusive photographers.
Make the practical difficulty concrete through missed appointments.
Distinguish a picture kept for remembrance from worship.
Keeps the short question and answer together: using moving pictures to present the history and persecution of the community.
Consider the association of photograph, prayer, and protection.
shortened: Thus if you desire protection from the powers of the world and earthly influences, place the Greatest Name in your dwelling, wear the ring of the Greatest Name, and keep Abdul Baha'is photograph in your home. Read my prayers always and thus see a wonderful effect, causing all superstitious powers and influences to vanish away.

order.why: Read a particular restriction with attention to its referent and setting.
shortened: Briefly: It is not permitted to hang the blessed photograph in rooms, however there is no harm in hanging the Greatest Name or "Ya Baha'u'l-Abha" or photographs of the Holy Shrine or photographs of places where Baha'u'llah resided.

order.why: A direct statement permitting photographs of the Blessed House to be taken and supplied to others.
Distinguishes an imaginary portrait attributed to the Bab from an authentic likeness.
Specifies the historical value of photographs and requests identification and accounts of the events depicted.
Close with the correction of a misidentified photograph.

questions: What helps an image deepen remembrance without becoming a substitute for understanding the person or teachings it represents?
How should affection for a figure be balanced with their expressed wishes about being photographed or having images distributed?
What difference do accurate identification, date, setting, and provenance make to the way we receive a photograph?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the responsibility involved in recording and transmitting a religious memory.
Explore the relation between an outward form and the meaning it is meant to serve.

references.label: 1 · Plato, Phaedrus 275d–276a — images that cannot answer
references.note: Near the dialogue’s end, Socrates compares writing to a painted figure that appears alive but cannot answer questions. Read the passage beginning with the comparison to painting. How might this limitation illuminate a photograph’s power and its dependence on reliable context, without diminishing its value as a remembrance?

subjects.displayTitle: Noah: steadfastness, mercy, and a new beginning
subjects.introduction: For nine hundred and fifty years, the tradition says, Noah called his people every day and was beaten for it with sticks and stones, and did not flag. The Bahá’í writings return to him as the figure of a voice that keeps calling when an answer seems impossible: promised victories that failed to arrive and shook his few followers, a son who was not of his family because his conduct was unrighteous, a flood that in one retelling is the drowning of the heedless in their own desires. In Bahá’u’lláh’s long account the angels twice stay Noah’s hand when he would call down affliction, bidding him have mercy on the weak, so that mercy precedes judgment for ages before the Ark of the Spirit is built. Genesis closes the story with a covenant that takes in every living creature under the sign of the rainbow [1], widening what a community understands itself to protect. The carpenter who built an ark of salvation becomes a pattern for any craftsman’s service. The way leads on into the Torah and the Jewish people, and into firmness in the Covenant.
subjects.arc: Hear the persistent call, confront the testing of faith, and follow the ark and flood into questions of mercy and spiritual kinship.

order.why: Consider expectation, delay, and the testing of followers.
shortened: Long afterward, He several times promised victory to His companions and fixed the hour thereof. But when the hour struck, the divine promise was not fulfilled. This caused a few among the small number of His followers to turn away from Him, and to this testify the records of the best-known books. These you must certainly have perused; if not, undoubtedly you will. Finally, as stated in books and traditions, there remained with Him only forty or seventy-two of His followers. At last from the depth of His being He cried aloud: "Lord! Leave not upon the land a single dweller from among the unbelievers."

order.why: Begin with the voice of a humble and persistent caller.
Encounter the sustained rejection described in the retelling.
shortened: His Holiness Noah (peace be upon him) called the people for nine hundred and fifty years each day, and they would abuse him so severely with sticks, clubs, fists, slaps, stones and whips that they were certain he would die. Despite this he did not flag or fall short.

order.why: Distinguish spiritual kinship from lineage alone.
Distinguishes historical accounts about Noah and other biblical figures from the divine laws, in a discussion of infallibility.
Introduce a spiritual reading of the flood.
Notice the invocation of Noah’s age in a prayer.
Uses differences between the laws of Noah, Abraham and Moses to explain changing human capacity.
Connect craftsmanship with the work of deliverance.
shortened: O thou who followest Noah the Carpenter! O carpenter! Thou art of the same craft and profession as His Holiness Noah. He built the ark of salvation and played the game of service at the Sacred Threshold. He protected a company of souls from the Most Great Flood and preserved them from destruction. Thou too must engage in service to the Ark of the Covenant, that thou mayest become the cause of salvation to all regions and attain, beneath the shelter of the effulgent light, to the greatest gifts of the Lord of the Day of Meeting.

order.why: Read the extended account of mercy, delay, and a spiritual ark.
shortened: Then We sent down to him the angels of heaven that he might be among those who show mercy, and they descended upon him and said: "O Noah, deal not with them as they have dealt with thee. Have mercy upon them and take them not to task for their rebellion, for they are weak upon the earth and poor in the kingdom, possessing neither death nor life nor resurrection for themselves.

When he heard the call of God, his soul was stirred with longing and he raised his hands, saying: "O my Lord! Leave not these people upon the earth." We answered his prayer and commanded him to build the Ark. When the Ark of the Spirit was completed through the Most Great Word, We said: "O Noah! Embark therein those of thy kindred for whom the decree hath already gone forth, those who excel in the religion of God." Then did We cause the clouds of wrath to rain down showers of heedlessness, and We drowned all who were on earth save those who were embarked upon the Ark of the Spirit.

order.why: A self-contained account of Noah's call, rejection, prayer and command to build the ark.
Close with a covenant oriented toward a future Manifestation.
shortened: Then when ages and epochs passed, We sent forth Noah from Our presence to guide people unto God and give them glad tidings of these days. We commanded him to take from the people of earth a covenant concerning this Manifestation.

At every moment he was afflicted with hardship and adversity in God's path - the King, the Powerful, the Most High, the All-Knowing - until We delivered him and those with him, and drowned the evil-doing people who were among the lost.

questions: What kind of steadfastness do these accounts attribute to Noah, and how does it differ from certainty about an immediate result?
How does the discussion of Noah’s son change the meaning of belonging to a spiritual family?
What tensions between mercy and judgment remain in these retellings, and what do they ask of a reader?
How do the spiritual ark and Genesis’s covenant with living creatures each broaden the meaning of deliverance?

neighbors.invitation: Consider a prayer that seeks an oppressor’s repentance.
Explore the image of humanity entering a new springtime.

references.label: 1 · Genesis 9:8–17 — a covenant with living creatures
references.note: After the flood, the covenant extends beyond Noah’s household to the living creatures, with the rainbow as its sign. Read this conclusion beside the compilation’s retellings of endurance and spiritual deliverance. Consider how the scope of a covenant changes what a community understands itself to protect.

subjects.introduction: When the disciples sat stunned before the crucified body of their Lord, it was Mary Magdalene who asked them whether they were mourning His body or His spirit, and told them that Jesus lives. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá returns to that scene whenever He explains the resurrection of Christ. For two or three days after the martyrdom the reality of Christ, His teachings and spiritual power, lay hidden, and His Cause was like a lifeless body; on the third day the apostles, steadied by one steadfast woman, arose to serve Him, and the religion of Christ rose with them. Heaven, in the same reading, is not the sky but the Kingdom of God, from which Christ came though born of Mary and to which He returned; the cloud on which He is awaited is the human body that veils the Sun of Truth; the fish and honeycomb eaten after Easter are symbols to be understood in the spirit. Luke, with his insistence on hands and feet, flesh and bones and a meal shared, states the other reading in its strongest form, and the two deserve to be held side by side with their difference intact [1]. From here the way leads to Mary Magdalene herself, to the crucifixion and ascension, and to the interpretation of scripture more widely.
subjects.arc: Begin with Mary Magdalene restoring courage, explore resurrection as the revival of the Cause, and consider spiritual presence beyond physical location.

order.why: Read the developed explanation of the Cause’s renewed life.
Begin with Mary Magdalene consoling and encouraging the disciples.
shortened: "Just as in the time of Christ: the disciples were agitated when they saw the body of Jesus crucified. Then Mary Magdalene came to them and said: 'Why are you agitated?' 'Because,' they replied, 'Jesus has been crucified.' 'Oh,' she said, 'that was the body of Jesus, but the Reality of Jesus is living and eternal. It is not subject to corruption.'

order.why: Interprets the three days following the crucifixion through the disciples' discouragement and renewed realization of the enduring Cause of Christ.
Return to the insight that revives their confidence.
Uses resurrection in a distinct dispensational sense: the appearance of a later Messenger brings the resurrection of the previous Revelation.
Consider the three days within this spiritual interpretation.
Attend to the recognition of Mary Magdalene’s greatness.
shortened: The greatness of her station was not known during her lifetime, but after nineteen hundred years God has made it clear that this woman was the most steadfast of all the followers of His Holiness Christ. After the crucifixion his disciples were greatly agitated, even Peter who, although he had denied His Holiness Christ to be, was considered the chief of the apostles, but this marvelous woman caused them to become firm and steadfast. Through the power of her faith they were able to see that though the body of Christ had been crucified yet his spirit or reality had not suffered but was with them still; that his body was like a torn and discarded garment, but that his spirit was eternal and indestructible. Thus the disciples became reorganized through her exhortations and exhibition of firmness.

order.why: Connect her role with the nonspatial meaning of heaven.
shortened: On the third day, Mary Magdalene became the cause of their steadfastness and firmness. The Cause of Christ rose again and His teachings were revived, for Mary Magdalene explained to the disciples that what had occurred affected only the body of Christ - nothing had befallen the reality of Christ. Christ was living and enduring, and was ascending to the heaven of reality.
By heaven is not meant the physical heaven but the spiritual heaven.

order.why: Examine the relation of spirit, body, heaven, and cloud.
shortened: Verily the heaven into which the Messiah rose up was not this unending sky, rather was His heaven the Kingdom of His beneficent Lord. Even as He Himself hath said, 'I came down from heaven,' and again, 'The Son of Man is in heaven.' Hence it is clear that His heaven is beyond all directional points; it encircleth all existence, and is raised up for those who worship God.

Rather, the cloud referred to in the Gospel is the human body, so called because the body is as a veil to man, which, even as a cloud, preventeth him from beholding the Sun of Truth that shineth from the horizon of Christ.

order.why: Consider heaven through the language of divine will.
Encounter the symbolic reading of eating after resurrection.
Close with spiritual influence and the capacity to receive it.

questions: What role does Mary Magdalene play in these accounts, and how does her action shape their meaning of resurrection?
What changes when the revival of a community’s faith is described as the rising of Christ’s Cause?
How would you state both the compilation’s interpretation and the challenge posed by Luke’s bodily language fairly, without erasing their difference?
What might an enduring spiritual presence make possible in a community facing loss, fear, or apparent defeat?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the explicit distinction between spiritual renewal and physical re-creation.
Explore a relationship to spiritual reality that cannot be measured in space.

references.label: 1 · Luke 24:36–43 — touch, recognition, and eating
references.note: Luke emphasizes the risen Jesus’ hands and feet, flesh and bones, and eating before the disciples. Read the narrative beside the compilation’s spiritual interpretation, especially its treatment of eating. What does each reading take the text to affirm, and what would each need to explain about the other’s evidence?
